title: CSC3710 2026-10-01: DFA to regex, closure under complement, non-regular languages

questions.q: In the paths-and-cycles table, each final state f gets one row. Which regular expression goes in the last column of that row?
choices: (union of the paths)(union of the cycles)*
(union of the paths)*(union of the cycles)
(union of the paths) ∪ (union of the cycles)*
(union of the paths)(union of the cycles)
questions.explain: Take any path from the initial state to f, then go around f's cycles in any order, as many times as you like (including zero). That is (∪ paths)(∪ cycles)*.

questions.q: A DFA has two final states, q3 and q4. You have built the row expressions R_q3 and R_q4. What is the regular expression for L(M)?
questions.explain: A string is accepted if it ends in q3 or ends in q4, so you take the union of the rows. The table is not the final answer. The union of its row expressions is.

questions.q: In the paths-and-cycles table, no cycle leaves a final state and comes back to it. What do you write in that row's Cycle(s) column?
questions.explain: Write λ. Giving the machine nothing leaves it where it is, so λ takes the state back to itself. Since λ* = λ, the row becomes (paths)λ* = paths.

questions.q: A path from the initial state to final state f passes through a middle state that has a self-loop. Where does that self-loop go in the table?
choices: In the Cycle(s) column for f
In a separate row of its own
Inside the path's regex, with a Kleene star
Nowhere, because only cycles on final states matter
questions.explain: A cycle at the beginning or in the middle of a path belongs in the path's regex, written with a star (for example a a* b). Only cycles on the final state itself go in the Cycle(s) column.

questions.q: True or false: f has a self-loop on b. Its Cycle(s) entry should list b, bb, bbb, and so on, to cover going around the loop several times.
questions.explain: The Cycle(s) column holds strings that take f back to f exactly once. The outer Kleene star over the union of cycles handles repetition.

questions.q: DFA over Σ = {a}: q0 --a--> q1, q1 --a--> q2, q2 --a--> q1. The initial state is q0 and the only final state is q1. What regular expression does the paths-and-cycles method give?
questions.explain: The path q0 to q1 is a. The cycle q1 to q2 to q1 is aa. So the row is a(aa)*, which is the odd-length strings. That is the same language as the 2-state odd-length DFA.

questions.q: DFA over Σ = {a, b}: q0 --a--> q1 and q0 --b--> q1. q1 is the only final state, and every other transition goes to a trap state. What does the method give?
questions.explain: There are two paths, a and b. No cycle leaves q1 and returns, so the cycle entry is λ. (a ∪ b)λ* = a ∪ b. The machine accepts exactly the strings a and b.

questions.q: DFA over {a, b}, initial state q0, only final state q2. Transitions: q0 --b--> q1, q1 --b--> q2, q2 --b--> q2, q2 --a--> q3, q3 --a--> q3, q3 --b--> q4, q4 --a--> q3, q4 --b--> q2. All other transitions go to a trap state. Its language is bb(b ∪ aa*b(aa*b)*b)*. A student leaves off the outer star and writes bb(b ∪ aa*b(aa*b)*b). Which strings does the machine accept that the student's expression misses?
questions.explain: Without the outer star you must go around exactly one cycle exactly once. bb uses zero cycles, bbbb uses green twice, and bbbabb uses green and then blue, so all three are missed. bbb (green once) and bbabb (blue once) are still matched. The outer star is what lets the machine switch between cycles.

questions.q: True or false: for any regular expressions r and s, (r ∪ s)* = (r* ∪ s)*.
questions.explain: Under an outer star over a union, you can add a star to either part, or to both: (r ∪ s)* = (r* ∪ s)* = (r ∪ s*)* = (r* ∪ s*)*. That is why putting a star on every cycle you see is still correct.

questions.q: The machine with only final state q2 (path bb, green self-loop b on q2, blue cycle aa*b(aa*b)*b) has language bb(b ∪ aa*b(aa*b)*b)*. Which of these also describe that language?
questions.explain: The extra b* in the first choice is redundant, because the starred union already allows any number of b's, but it is not an error. The second choice follows from (r ∪ s)* = (r* ∪ s)*. The third has no outer star. The fourth does not allow a green b after a blue cycle, so it misses bbabbb.

questions.q: In that same machine, the blue cycle from q2 back to q2 has the regex a a* b (a a* b)* b. What does the (a a* b)* part capture?
choices: Going around the green self-loop on q2 any number of times
Going back from q4 to q3 (with the a-loop at q3) and returning to q4, zero or more times
Going around the whole blue cycle more than once
The path from the initial state to q2
questions.explain: After a a* b, the machine is at q4. From there it can take a back to q3, loop on a, then take b back to q4, as many times as it likes or not at all. The final b then returns it to q2.

questions.q: JFLAP exports a regular expression containing a+b. What does + mean in JFLAP's output?
questions.explain: JFLAP uses + for union, so a+b means a ∪ b. In our course notation, a+ means aa* (one or more), and JFLAP has no symbol for that. The online regex tool uses | for union.

questions.q: You compare your regular expression with JFLAP's in a regex comparison tool. It lists bbabb as "accepted by first but not second." What does that tell you?
choices: The two expressions are not equivalent, and bbabb is a counterexample you can trace through the machine to find the mistake
Only bbabb differs, so the expressions are equivalent apart from one string
The machine is not a DFA
questions.explain: A single string accepted by one expression and not the other proves they differ. Trace that string through the DFA to see which expression is wrong. In lecture this showed that an a had been typed where a b belonged.

questions.q: Which of these are equivalent to ▲▲▲▲(▲▲▲)* (4, 7, 10, ... triangles)?
questions.explain: Every piece uses only triangles, so the order of concatenation does not change the language. ▲(▲▲▲)+ gives 1 + 3m triangles with m ≥ 1, which is 4, 7, 10, .... ▲▲▲▲▲* allows any count of 4 or more. (▲▲▲▲)* gives multiples of 4. ▲(▲▲▲)* also allows a single triangle.

questions.q: True or false: every DFA must have at least one final state.
questions.explain: The definition only requires exactly one transition for each symbol out of every state. A DFA with no final states is valid and accepts the empty language ∅.

questions.q: Over {a, b}, every state of a machine has exactly one a-arrow and one b-arrow leaving it, but its only final state cannot be reached from the initial state. Which statement is correct?
choices: It is not a DFA, because a DFA's final states must be reachable
It is a DFA, and it accepts every string
It is a DFA, and it accepts no strings (the empty language)
It is not a DFA, because it has a useless state
questions.explain: Nothing in the definition requires final states to be reachable, so it is a DFA. No run can end in the final state, so the language is ∅. It is equivalent to a DFA with no final states at all.

questions.q: What languages can a DFA with exactly one state accept?
choices: Either every string over Σ or no strings
Any regular language over a one-symbol alphabet
questions.explain: The single state is both the start state and the state every run ends in. If it is final, every string is accepted. If not, nothing is.

questions.q: What is the smallest number of states a DFA over Σ = {a} can have if it accepts exactly the odd-length strings?
questions.explain: The language accepts some strings and rejects others, so one state cannot be enough (one state accepts everything or nothing). A 2-state machine does it.

questions.q: True or false: a 3-state DFA and a 2-state DFA over {a} can both accept exactly the odd-length strings.
questions.explain: A DFA may have more states than it needs, much like code that is not optimized. The 3-state machine q0 --a--> q1, q1 --a--> q2, q2 --a--> q1 with final state q1 accepts a(aa)*, the same language as the 2-state machine.

questions.q: Which condition describes when a DFA accepts an infinite language?
choices: The initial state is final and has a self-loop
The DFA contains at least one cycle somewhere
There is a path from the initial state to some final state with a cycle on it
The DFA has more than two states
questions.explain: The cycle has to be reachable from the initial state, and some final state has to be reachable after it. The cycle can be at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end of the path. An initial final state with a self-loop is only one example of this.

questions.q: True or false: if a DFA's only cycle is the self-loop on its trap state, the DFA accepts an infinite language.
questions.explain: No final state can be reached from a trap state, so that cycle never lies on a path to a final state. With no other cycle, only finitely many strings can be accepted.

questions.q: What does "the set of regular languages is closed under complement" mean?
choices: If L is regular, then its complement Σ* − L is also regular
If L is regular, then its complement is not regular
The complement of any language is regular
A regular language contains its own complement
questions.explain: Applying the operation (complement) to a member of the set (a regular language) always gives another member of the set. So for the complement you can always build a DFA or write a regular expression.

questions.q: True or false: the set of integers is closed under division.
questions.explain: 1 ÷ 2 is not an integer. The integers are closed under addition and multiplication but not under division. This is the same idea of closure as "regular languages are closed under complement."

questions.q: M = (Q, Σ, δ, q0, F) is a DFA with L(M) = L. Which machine accepts the complement of L?
questions.explain: Keep everything the same except the final states: states that were not final become final, and states that were final stop being final. Each string has exactly one run, ending in one state, so M′ accepts exactly the strings M rejects.

questions.q: A DFA has Q = {q0, q1, q2, q3} and F = {q1, q3}. What is the set of final states of the DFA that accepts the complement?
questions.explain: The complement machine's final states are Q − F = {q0, q2}.

questions.q: Over Σ = {a}, L = (aa)*, the even-length strings. Which regular expression describes the complement of L?
questions.explain: Every string is either odd or even length, so the complement of the even-length strings is the odd-length strings, a(aa)*.

questions.q: Over Σ = {a, b}, you derive a regex for L(M), flip M's final states to get M′, derive a regex for L(M′), and take the union of the two. What language do you get?
questions.explain: L(M′) is the complement of L(M), and L ∪ (Σ* − L) = Σ*. For Σ = {a}, the same idea gives (aa)* ∪ a(aa)* = a*.

questions.q: You already have a DFA for strings that start with bb and end with bb. What is the easiest way to get a DFA for strings that do NOT (start with bb and end with bb)?
choices: Design a new machine from scratch
Reverse every arrow in the existing machine
Swap final and non-final states in the existing machine
questions.explain: The new language is the complement of the old one, so flipping the final states (Q − F) gives the machine directly. Sometimes it is easier to design the complement first and then flip it.

questions.q: A DFA M over Σ has no final states. You flip its final states to build M′. What does M′ accept?
choices: Nothing, because M was not a valid DFA
questions.explain: M accepts ∅. M′ has final states Q − ∅ = Q, so every run ends in a final state and M′ accepts Σ*, the complement of ∅.

questions.q: Which of these makes a language regular?
choices: It is a subset of Σ*
It is described by a regular expression or accepted by a DFA
Its strings can be listed in order of length
questions.explain: A language described by a regular expression is regular, and so is a language accepted by a DFA. Being a subset of Σ* only makes it a language.

questions.q: A language over Σ is any subset of Σ*. What is the set of all languages over Σ?
choices: P(Σ*), the power set of Σ*
P(Σ), the power set of Σ
questions.explain: Every subset of Σ* is a language, so the collection of all of them is the power set P(Σ*). The regular languages are one region inside it.

questions.q: True or false: { aⁱbⁱ | i ≥ 0 } is a regular language.
questions.explain: It is not regular, and there is a proof that no DFA accepts it. It is an example of a context-free language.

questions.q: Which strings are in a*b* but NOT in { aⁱbⁱ | i ≥ 0 }?
questions.explain: a*b* allows any number of a's followed by any number of b's, with nothing tying the two counts together. aab, b, and abb have unequal counts. ab and aabb have equal counts, so they are in both. This is why a*b* does not describe aⁱbⁱ.

questions.q: Programming languages are context-free, like { aⁱbⁱ | i ≥ 0 }. Which feature gives the intuition for this?
choices: Keywords come from a fixed finite list
The number of opening parentheses must match the number of closing ones, in the right order
Identifiers are made of letters and digits
questions.explain: Matching opening and closing parentheses ties two counts together, as one i controls both the a's and the b's in aⁱbⁱ. A parser checks this.

questions.q: L = { ♥ⁱ ●²ʲ ▲³ᵏ⁺¹ | i ≥ 1, j ≥ 0, k ≥ 1 }. What is the shortest string in L?
questions.explain: Use the smallest values: i = 1 gives one heart, j = 0 gives no circles, and k = 1 gives 3(1) + 1 = 4 triangles. That is ♥▲▲▲▲, length 5.

questions.q: L = { ♥ⁱ ●²ʲ ▲³ᵏ⁺¹ | i ≥ 1, j ≥ 0, k ≥ 1 }. Which strings are in L?
questions.explain: ♥●●▲▲▲▲▲▲▲: i = 1, j = 1, and 7 triangles means k = 2, so it is in L. ♥♥▲▲▲▲: i = 2, j = 0, k = 1, so it is in L. ♥●▲▲▲▲ has an odd number of circles. ●●▲▲▲▲ has no hearts, but i ≥ 1. ♥▲ has 1 triangle, but k ≥ 1 requires at least 4.

questions.q: Which regular expression describes L = { ♥ⁱ ●²ʲ ▲³ᵏ⁺¹ | i ≥ 1, j ≥ 0, k ≥ 1 }?
questions.explain: ♥♥* gives one or more hearts, (●●)* gives an even number of circles (possibly zero), and ▲▲▲▲(▲▲▲)* gives 4, 7, 10, ... triangles. The first choice allows zero hearts, the second allows an odd number of circles, and the last allows a single triangle (k = 0).

questions.q: Intuitively, why is { ♥ⁱ ●²ʲ ▲³ᵏ⁺¹ | i ≥ 1, j ≥ 0, k ≥ 1 } regular while { aⁱbⁱ | i ≥ 0 } is not?
choices: The first uses three symbols and the second uses only two
In the first, each count has its own variable. In the second, one variable controls both counts, so they must stay in sync
questions.explain: The numbers of hearts, circles, and triangles do not depend on each other. In aⁱbⁱ the same i sets both the a's and the b's, and a DFA or regular expression cannot keep two counts in sync.
